text: Late that night. <break time="0.8s" /> As Bernice passed her aunts door. <break time="0.8s" /> She heard her own name and stopped. <break time="0.8s" /> Unable to resist listening. <break time="0.8s" /> To the conversation inside. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie was complaining to her mother. <break time="0.8s" /> That Bernice was hopeless. <break time="0.8s" /> And that no boy would ever take an interest. <break time="0.8s" /> In such a dull, awkward girl. <break time="0.8s" /> Missus Harvey tried to defend her niece. <break time="0.8s" /> But Marjorie replied. <break time="0.8s" /> That being nice and polite meant nothing to boys. <break time="0.8s" /> If a girl had no charm. <break time="0.8s" /> The next morning. <break time="0.8s" /> Bernice accused her cousin. <break time="0.8s" /> Of being cruel. <break time="0.8s" /> And she threatened. <break time="0.8s" /> To go home to Eau Claire at once. <break time="0.8s" /> If she was not wanted. <break time="0.8s" /> Instead of apologizing. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie coolly answered. <break time="0.8s" /> That her cousin was free to leave. <break time="0.8s" /> Since she had made no effort. <break time="0.8s" /> To be pleasant company. <break time="0.8s" /> When Bernice spoke. <break time="0.8s" /> Of the gentle, womanly girls in Little Women. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie laughed and declared. <break time="0.8s" /> That such old fashioned ideals. <break time="0.8s" /> No longer belonged in the modern world. <break time="0.8s" /> Shaken but secretly impressed. <break time="0.8s" /> Bernice swallowed her pride and asked. <break time="0.8s" /> Will you tell me what is wrong with me. <break time="0.8s" /> And how I can change it. <break time="0.8s" /> Marjorie agreed to help her. <break time="0.8s" /> But only on one condition. <break time="0.8s" /> That Bernice would do exactly. <break time="0.8s" /> What she was told. <break time="0.8s" /> Without arguing or asking why.
